sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Bernoulli Trials
sections.content: Define a 'Bernoulli Trial' as a single experiment with exactly two outcomes: Success (p) or Failure (1-p). Visualize this as a simple coin flip animation: Head (Success) vs. Tail (Failure).
sections.example: Flipping a fair coin: Head (Success, p=0.5), Tail (Failure, q=0.5).

sections.title: Defining the Binomial Conditions (BINS)
sections.content: Introduce the BINS mnemonic: Binary (two outcomes), Independent (trials don't affect each other), Number (fixed number of trials 'n'), Success (constant probability 'p'). Use a checklist visual to emphasize these constraints.
sections.example: A basketball player shooting 10 free throws; each shot is independent with a fixed 70% success rate.

sections.title: The Binomial Formula Breakdown
sections.content: Explain the formula: P(X=k) = C(n,k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Break it down visually: C(n,k) represents the number of ways to arrange successes, while p^k * (1-p)^(n-k) represents the probability of a specific sequence.
sections.example: Using the combination tree: Calculating the probability of getting exactly 2 heads in 3 tosses.

sections.title: Visualizing the Probability Distribution
sections.content: Display a dynamic bar chart that changes shape as 'n' and 'p' parameters are adjusted. Show how the distribution shifts and becomes more symmetric as 'n' increases (Central Limit Theorem hint).
sections.example: Animation showing 5, 10, and 20 tosses; watch the 'bell curve' shape emerge for 100 trials.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
sections.content: Apply the concept to a factory scenario. Calculate the probability of having 'k' defective devices in a batch to demonstrate how companies use this to maintain quality standards.
sections.example: A robot arm on an assembly line has a 2% defect rate. Calculate the probability of finding exactly 1 defective unit in a batch of 50.
